threads.thread_goal: Align on scope and pick which vehicles join the initial pilot

messages.text: Kicking off the Fleet Maintenance and Workshop Safety Standardization project (project_pack_ref: Fleet Maintenance and Workshop Safety Standardization). Goal is to test the new routines on a small group of vehicles before we roll out to the whole fleet. For the pilot linked to T10, we need to pick which vehicle types and how many units, and agree how long we run it. My first thought is to focus on the highest-usage collection trucks so we see issues quickly and can feed them into the maintenance schedule layout in A3 and the weekly routine in T2. Can you share which vehicles you think should be in the first batch and any constraints from your shifts?

From the last month of breakdowns, the rear-loader collection trucks on the early shift seem to give us the most trouble, especially the ones on the glass routes. I suggest we include 3 of those plus 2 side-loaders that run almost every day. That would give us the 5 vehicles we need for T10 without blocking the whole operation. We can map them clearly on the board layout in A3 so all shifts see which ones are under the new routine.

On late shift we see more issues with the smaller cage trucks that do the city centre runs. They come back with a lot of minor damage and loose wiring. Should we add at least one of those to the pilot so we do not miss that pattern? Not sure if that would be too many vehicles though.

If we add a cage truck, maybe we can still keep the total at 5 by dropping one of the side-loaders. That way we cover three types: rear-loader, side-loader, and cage. It might give us better data for T2 when we estimate weekly deep-check times by type.

From my side on the weekend shift, the rear-loaders are the ones that come in dirty and rushed. I like the idea of focusing on them. I am fine if we keep 3 rear-loaders and 1 side-loader and 1 cage truck like suggested. I just want to be sure we do not pick trucks that are always in the workshop already, or we will not see the real impact.

So far I am hearing: 3 high-usage rear-loaders on glass routes, 1 side-loader, 1 cage truck. Total 5 vehicles, which matches the minimum in T10. That gives us a good spread without overloading us. Unless anyone objects, I will treat that as our pilot set and mark them on the schedule board layout in A3 with a simple label so they stand out.

Works for me. For duration, I suggest we run the pilot for one full week of operations, including at least one weekend day. That way we see how the routines behave on busy days and quieter days. We can log any delays or issues as required in T10 and then summarise them before we adjust the weekly routine in T2.

One week sounds ok, but we should avoid starting on a public holiday week. Maybe we start next Monday so we get a normal pattern. That gives us a few days to prepare the board in line with A3 and brief the drivers.

Agree with starting next Monday. We can use the rest of this week to double-check that the daily checklist draft in A1 and the weekly routine draft in T2 are ready enough for a pilot, even if they are not final. Otherwise we will be testing something that changes every day.

Just to confirm, during the pilot week we still follow the current checks for the rest of the fleet, right? Only these 5 trucks get the new routine from T10 and the others stay as they are until we review the results.

Yes, correct. Only the 5 pilot vehicles follow the new routines from T10. All other vehicles stay on the current process until we review the pilot summary. We will make that clear on the board using the layout in A3 so no one is confused at shift start.

To capture the impact properly, we should agree what we log during the pilot. I suggest we note: extra minutes spent on checks per vehicle, any missed collections due to the new steps, and any defects we caught earlier than usual. That will help when we refine T2 and when we fill the feedback summary in A8 later.

I can keep a simple note for late shift with those three points for each of the 5 vehicles. Maybe early shift can do the same so we see differences between shifts. We can then combine them into the pilot feedback summary in A8.

One more thing: we should check with the fleet supervisor about any vehicles already booked for longer repairs next week. If one of the chosen 5 is going to be off the road for days, we might want to swap it before we lock in the list for T10.

Good point. I will check the upcoming repairs with the fleet supervisor this afternoon and confirm the final list of 5 vehicles. If any of the suggested ones are unavailable, I will pick a similar route and type so the pilot still covers the same mix.

To be explicit: proposal is pilot duration of 1 calendar week, starting next Monday at first shift and ending after last shift on Sunday. After that we take one or two days to compile the notes into A8 and adjust T2 if needed. Any objections to that timing?
No objection from me. Starting Monday for one week is fine. It will help me get used to the new checks without changing everything at once.
Fine by me as well. I will adjust my end-of-shift notes so we clearly mark which comments are from the pilot vehicles.

Sounds like we have agreement. We will run the pilot on 5 vehicles (3 rear-loaders on glass routes, 1 side-loader, 1 cage truck) for one full week starting next Monday. I will confirm the exact vehicle IDs after checking repairs and then update the board layout in A3 accordingly. We will log delays and early defect catches as part of T10 so we can feed them into T2 and A8 later.

threads.thread_goal: Draft and finalise the daily inspection checklist and weekly routine

messages.text: I have put together a first draft of the daily vehicle inspection checklist based on our current practice and the project goals. It is saved as A1 and linked to T1. Sections are: exterior walk-around, cab and controls, fluids, tyres and wheels, and safety equipment. Some items like detailed brake checks might belong in the weekly routine under T2 instead of daily. Please review and comment on anything missing, too heavy for daily, or better suited to weekly.

Thanks for drafting A1. First impression: the structure is clear and matches how we move around the vehicle. For daily checks, I think we should definitely keep lights, indicators, horn, mirrors, visible leaks, tyre damage, and basic safety kit. The detailed inspection of suspension and full underbody might be better in the weekly deep-check in T2, otherwise we will slow down turnaround too much.

Looking at A1, I am wondering about the fluids section. Right now it has engine oil, coolant, washer fluid, and hydraulic oil. On busy mornings we struggle to check all of those on every truck. Maybe we can keep coolant and visible leaks daily, and move full hydraulic oil level checks to the weekly routine in T2?

I noticed the checklist in A1 has a step for checking all warning lights on the dash with ignition on. Do we need to write down what each light means, or is it enough to say report any light that stays on? I sometimes forget the names of some of them.

Maybe we can keep the daily checklist in A1 simple and add a small legend with icons on the wall near the board layout in A3. That way the checklist just says check for any warning lights staying on, and the legend helps people recognise them without making A1 too long.

Good point on fluids. For daily, I suggest we keep: coolant level, visible leaks under the vehicle, and washer fluid if time allows. Engine oil and hydraulic oil can be checked visually daily on the pilot vehicles, but the full top-up and detailed check can move to the weekly routine in T2. That way we still spot big issues early without opening every panel every morning.

I agree with that split. For tyres, I would keep daily checks to visible damage, obvious low pressure, and wheel nut indicators where fitted. Detailed tread depth measurement can go into the weekly deep-check in T2. That should keep the daily checklist in A1 under 10 minutes per vehicle in normal conditions.

For safety equipment, I think daily we should confirm presence of fire extinguisher, first aid kit, and warning triangle, plus that the reversing alarm works. Checking expiry dates on extinguishers and full contents of the first aid kit could be weekly under T2.

I like the idea of the legend on the wall. For the daily checklist in A1, could we also add a simple yes or no box for each section so it is clear if we did it? Sometimes I forget to tick individual items when there are too many lines.

We can group items into blocks in A1: exterior, cab, fluids, tyres, safety. Each block gets a yes or no and a space for notes. That keeps it short and still auditable for T1. Detailed notes can go into the incident log in A4 if we find something serious.

I will update A1 with: grouped sections with yes or no boxes, a short notes field, and a clear split between daily items and those moved to the weekly routine in T2. For the weekly list, I will start a separate draft under T2 that includes detailed brake checks, full fluid levels, suspension, underbody, and tyre tread depth.

When you draft the weekly routine for T2, please also estimate time per vehicle by type using what we discussed in TH1. That will help us plan slots on the board layout in A3 and avoid clashing with peak collection hours.

One question: do we want the weekly deep-check in T2 to be done on a fixed day for each vehicle, or just within a 7-day window? Fixed days might be easier to show on A3, but a window gives us more flexibility when something urgent comes in.
Maybe we can set a target day for each vehicle on A3 but allow a plus or minus one day window. That way we keep some structure without forcing a deep-check on a day when the truck is urgently needed.

I like the target day with a small window. I will reflect that in the T2 draft and add a note that the board in A3 should show the target day and a colour change when we are close to overdue. For now, I want to confirm that everyone is comfortable with the structure of A1: grouped sections, daily items limited to quick visual and functional checks, and heavier checks moved to T2.
Yes, that structure works for me. The grouped sections and yes or no boxes will make it easier to follow at the start of shift.
I am ok with that too. Moving the detailed checks to T2 should keep the daily routine realistic while still catching big issues.

Agreed. The updated A1 layout and the split between daily and weekly checks make sense and should be easy to train. Once you finalise the edits, we can treat A1 as the standard daily checklist and use it in the pilot.

Great, I will lock in the A1 structure and complete the T2 weekly deep-check draft with the items we moved over: detailed brakes, full fluid levels, suspension, underbody, tyre tread depth, and safety kit expiry checks. I will also estimate time per vehicle type so we can plug it into A3.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on hazardous substances handling rules and workshop standards

messages.text: Starting a thread on hazardous substances and workshop standards. I drafted some initial ideas for the handling and storage guide under T3, which will become A2, and for cleaning and tool storage standards under T9, which will become A6. Proposal: 1) all oils, degreasers, and cleaning agents labelled and stored in marked zones; 2) clear PPE rules by substance; 3) simple spill response steps; 4) end-of-shift cleaning checklist and fixed locations for tools. Please share what works or does not work from your shifts so we can finalise A2 and A6.

On late shift we often find open containers of degreaser left on benches. In A2 I suggest we add a rule that all chemical containers must be closed and returned to the chemical zone immediately after use, no exceptions. For A6, we can mark that zone clearly on the floor and on shelves so it is obvious where things go.

For PPE, could A2 include a simple table: for each common substance (engine oil, hydraulic oil, brake cleaner, degreaser, battery acid), list required gloves, eye protection, and any extra like apron? That would make it easier for new staff to follow without reading long text.
Sometimes I am not sure where to put used rags soaked with oil or cleaner. Can we include in A2 and A6 a clear rule and a labelled bin for oily rags so they do not end up in general waste?

For spill response, I suggest A2 defines three simple steps: 1) stop the source if safe; 2) contain with absorbent from the spill kit; 3) dispose of used absorbent in the correct waste container. We should also specify who to inform and where to log the incident in A4 if the spill is significant.

Agree. We should also define in A6 that spill kits have a fixed location and are checked at least weekly, maybe as part of the deep-check routine in T2 or the cleaning standard in T9. Empty kits are a common problem.

On workshop organisation, I propose in A6 we define three zones: tools, chemicals, and waste. Tools on shadow boards or marked drawers, chemicals in a closed cabinet or marked shelves, and waste in clearly labelled bins (general, metal, oily rags, filters). End-of-shift cleaning in T9 can then say each zone must be left clear and bins not overflowing.

For the end-of-shift cleaning in T9, could we keep it to a short list so it is realistic? Maybe: clear floors of tools and parts, wipe up any spills, return tools to boards, empty small waste bins if full, and check that chemical containers are closed.

That sounds reasonable. We can put those steps into A6 as the standard and link them to T9. For hazardous substances in A2, we should also mention that decanting into unlabelled bottles is not allowed. All containers must have the original label or a clear secondary label.
We should also align A2 with the health and safety officer before final sign-off, especially on PPE and storage rules. I can send them the draft once we agree internally.

Good call. I will take responsibility for sending A2 to the health and safety officer once we are happy with it here. For now, can we confirm the key rules for A2: labelled storage zones, PPE table by substance, no unlabelled containers, simple three-step spill response, and clear disposal routes for oily rags and other waste?
I am happy with those rules for A2. They cover the main issues we see day to day and are simple enough to remember.
Works for me too, especially the part about clear bins for oily rags and other waste. That will help a lot.

I agree as well. For A6 and T9, can we also confirm that each shift is responsible for leaving the workshop in that standard state, not just the last shift of the day? Otherwise the early shift always ends up cleaning up.

Yes, A6 should state that the end-of-shift cleaning steps in T9 apply to every shift. We can keep the list short as discussed so it is realistic: clear floors, wipe spills, return tools, close containers, and check bins. That way the workshop stays consistent across the day.

Based on this, I will update A2 with the agreed hazardous substances rules and A6 with the cleaning and tool storage standards linked to T9. Once updated, I will send A2 to the health and safety officer for sign-off. Unless there are objections, we can treat these as our standard rules going into the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Define how incidents, near-misses and 'do not use' vehicles are flagged

messages.text: Yesterday we had a minor incident: during a check, I found a loose hydraulic hose on one of the rear-loaders. No spill, but it could have failed on the road. I tightened it and noted it in my notebook, but I was not sure how to log it properly or how clearly to mark the truck as not to be used until checked. With T5 and A4 in mind, how do we want to record this kind of near-miss and how should we flag a 'do not use' vehicle as part of T11?

Good example. For A4, I propose we always log near-misses like that, even if we fix them on the spot. Fields could be: date and time, vehicle ID, location (yard, workshop, on route), type (incident or near-miss), short description, immediate action taken, and who was informed. That would meet T5 and help us spot patterns.

On the 'do not use' side for T11, I suggest we define clear criteria: any safety-critical defect (brakes, steering, major fluid leak, loose wheel nuts, serious hydraulic issue) means the vehicle must not leave the yard until repaired or cleared by a supervisor. For your hose case, if there was any doubt about the fix, it should have been marked as not to be used.

Sometimes I am not sure if something is safety-critical or not. Could A4 or the T11 process include a short list of examples, like brake warning light on, big oil leak, steering play, so we know when to definitely mark 'do not use'?

We can add a simple reference list to the T11 procedure and post it near the board. For the visual method, I suggest we use a bright red magnetic tag on the board layout in A3 and a matching red tag on the vehicle key. If the tag is on, the vehicle is not to be used.

I like the red tag idea. For T11 we can define the steps: 1) mark the vehicle as 'do not use' on the board in A3 with a red magnet; 2) attach a red tag to the key; 3) write a short note on the board with the reason; 4) log the issue in A4 if it is an incident or near-miss; 5) inform the fleet supervisor.
For A4, do we want a free text description only, or also a simple category like mechanical, electrical, bodywork, slip or trip, chemical spill? Categories might help when we review logs later.
Good idea. We can add a simple category field to A4 with a short list as you suggested. That will still keep T5 simple but make the weekly review easier when we get to T12.
If a vehicle is marked 'do not use' with the red tag, who is allowed to remove the tag once it is fixed? I want to avoid someone just taking it off without checking properly.

We should say in T11 that only the fleet supervisor or a designated senior attendant can remove the red tag and clear the vehicle on A3, after confirming the repair. That keeps the decision with someone accountable.

Agree. I will check with the fleet supervisor, but the default in T11 can be that they or their delegate remove the tag. For us, the rule is simple: if the red tag is on the board or key, the vehicle does not leave the yard.
Back to A4, should we log very small things like a missing mirror cap, or only items that could have caused harm or damage? I do not want the log to become so full that people stop reading it.

I would say A4 is for anything that had or could have had safety, environmental, or major operational impact. Cosmetic issues like small scratches can stay in normal maintenance notes. We can add that guidance into T5 so people know what belongs in the log.

For my hose example, based on what we said, I should have: marked the truck as 'do not use' with a red tag, logged it in A4 as a near-miss with category mechanical, and told the supervisor. That helps me understand the new process.

To summarise: for A4 and T5 we will use fields date and time, vehicle ID, location, type (incident or near-miss), category, description, immediate action, and who was informed. For T11 we will use red tags on the board in A3 and on keys, with clear criteria for when to apply them and only the supervisor or delegate allowed to remove them. Is everyone ok with that as our standard?
Yes, that works for me. It is clear enough to follow even when it is busy.
I am aligned as well. The combination of A4 and the red tag process in T11 should make it much harder for serious issues to slip through.
Same here. Once A4 is set up, we should also make sure it is easy to access from all shifts, maybe a shared folder or a binder in the workshop, as part of T5.

Great, I will finalise A4 with the agreed fields and document the red tag process in T11, then share both for a quick check with the fleet supervisor. We will use these as the standard for logging incidents and marking 'do not use' vehicles during the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Plan training, shift handovers and weekly review cadence

messages.text: To support the new routines, we need to align on training for new staff, shift handovers, and a weekly review. I drafted a simple handover notes template under T6 that will become A5, and a short training brief under T8 that will become A7. For weekly reviews under T12, we also have the pilot feedback summary in A8. Proposal: 1) handover notes filled at end of every shift; 2) a short onboarding session for new attendants using A7; 3) a fixed weekly review slot to look at A3 and A4. Thoughts?

Looking at the handover template in A5, I like the sections for open issues, priorities, and parts on order. I suggest we add a small box for 'vehicles on do not use status' so it lines up with T11 and the red tags on A3. That way the next shift sees it in writing as well as on the board.

For when to fill A5, I think it should be mandatory at the end of every shift, even if there is not much to say. A quick 'no open issues' note is better than leaving it blank. Otherwise the next shift is never sure if something was missed.

In the training brief draft A7, there is a lot of information. For new starters, could we keep it to the basics: daily checklist A1, where to find the board A3, how to use the handover notes A5, and who to ask if they are unsure about a defect?
Agree. A7 should stay under two pages as T8 says. We can keep the main body simple and use links or references to A2, A6, and A4 for more detail once they are comfortable with the basics.

Good suggestion. I will add a 'do not use vehicles' box to A5 and keep the rest of the template to one page. For T6, we can say the handover must be filled at the end of each shift and quickly reviewed by the incoming shift at the start.

On the weekly review under T12, I propose we set a fixed slot mid-week, for example Wednesday at 10:00, when workload is usually manageable. Attendees should be at least one attendant from each shift plus the fleet supervisor when available. We will review A3, A4, and any notes from A8 during the pilot.

Wednesday 10:00 works for late shift as long as we rotate who attends so people are not always staying late. Maybe we can say each shift sends one representative to the T12 review, and we rotate that person every month.
For A5, could we also have a small space for 'parts expected next shift' so we know if we should wait for a delivery before starting a job?

In the weekly review, we should always look at at least two things: 1) overdue services or upcoming peaks on A3; 2) repeated incident types in A4. That will help us agree on at least two improvement actions as required by T12.

Yes, good call. I will add a 'parts expected' line to A5. That should help avoid surprises at the start of shift. With that, A5 will have: open issues, priorities, do not use vehicles, parts on order and expected, and any notes for the next shift.

For A7, I suggest we structure it into four short sections: 1) daily checks using A1; 2) using the schedule board A3; 3) how to read and fill handover notes A5; 4) when and how to log incidents in A4 and follow hazardous substance rules in A2 and A6. That should stay within the T8 limit and cover the essentials.
That layout for A7 works for me. For delivery, maybe we can do a 20 to 30 minute walkthrough on their first day, then a quick follow-up after one week to answer questions.
Just to be clear, if there is nothing special to report, should we write 'no open issues' in A5 or just tick a box? I prefer something simple so it does not slow us down.
We can add a small 'no open issues' tick box at the top of A5. If you tick it, you do not need to fill the rest unless there is something specific. That should keep T6 practical.

On the weekly review timing, does anyone see a problem with Wednesday 10:00 as the standard T12 slot, with one representative per shift and the fleet supervisor invited? If not, we can lock that in and start next week once the pilot begins.
No issues from me. Wednesday 10:00 is fine, and rotating the representative per shift makes sense.
Works for me too. I can take the first late-shift slot for the T12 review.

Given the feedback, I will finalise A5 with the sections we agreed and confirm in T6 that it must be filled at the end of every shift, with the incoming shift reviewing it at the start. That should give us consistent handovers.

To wrap up: we will use A5 as the standard handover template, filled at the end of every shift as part of T6, and we will set Wednesday 10:00 as the weekly review slot under T12 with one representative per shift plus the fleet supervisor. A7 will be the short training brief for new staff under T8, focusing on A1, A3, A5, A4, A2, and A6. I will share the updated A5 and A7 drafts for a quick final look, then send A7 to the operations manager or delegate for review as required by T8.
